q-250411.name: Question 1
q-250411.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{{2}^{5x}}{k}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{2}^{5y}}{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{2}^{5y}}{k} \\ kx & ={2}^{5y} \\ {2}^{5y} & =kx \\ {log}_{2}⁡({2}^{5y}) & ={log}_{2}⁡(kx) \\ 5y & ={log}_{2}⁡(kx) \\ y & =\frac{{log}_{2}⁡(kx)}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is ${f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{{log}_{2}⁡(kx)}{5}.$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that $k=7.$

q-228736.name: Question 2
q-228736.problem: The inverse of the function $f(x)={e}^{3x}$ is ${f}^{-1}(x)=${{field-1}}.
q-228736.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={e}^{3y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={e}^{3y} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{3y}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x & =3y \\ 3y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ y & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is ${f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}.$

q-228738.name: Question 3
q-228738.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {4}^{3x}-5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {4}^{3y}-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {4}^{3y}-5 \\ \frac{1}{2}\cdot {4}^{3y} & =x+5 \\ {4}^{3y} & =2x+10 \\ {log}_{4}⁡({4}^{3y}) & ={log}_{4}⁡(2x+10) \\ 3y & ={log}_{4}⁡(2x+10) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}{log}_{4}⁡(2x+10)\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is ${f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{3}{log}_{4}⁡(2x+10).$

q-250419.name: Question 4
q-250419.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot {8}^{5x-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot {8}^{5y-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot {8}^{5y-2} \\ \frac{1}{7}\cdot {8}^{5y-2} & =x \\ {8}^{5y-2} & =7x \\ {log}_{8}⁡({8}^{5y-2}) & ={log}_{8}⁡(7x) \\ 5y-2 & ={log}_{8}⁡(7x) \\ 5y & ={log}_{8}⁡(7x)+2 \\ y & =\frac{{log}_{8}⁡(7x)+2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is ${f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{{log}_{8}⁡(7x)+2}{5}.$

q-250483.name: Question 5
q-250483.problem: The inverse of the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}{log}_{2}⁡(x)+\frac{1}{2}$ is ${f}^{-1}(x)=${{field-1}}.
q-250483.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}{log}_{2}⁡(x)+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}{log}_{2}⁡(y)+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:        

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}{log}_{2}⁡(y)+\frac{1}{2} \\ x-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}{log}_{2}⁡y \\ 2x-1 & ={log}_{2}⁡y \\ {2}^{2x-1} & ={2}^{{log}_{2}⁡y} \\ {2}^{2x-1} & =y \\ y & ={2}^{2x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is ${f}^{-1}(x)={2}^{2x-1}.$
